title: Master Class | Ruy Lopez | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We play e5 for once — we haven't gone for it much this speedrun, even though it's what most people play.
White develops the knight to f3, hitting our pawn.
We defend with a knight to c6.
A bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez.
We head for the main line with a6, questioning the bishop.
White retreats to a4.
And we develop the knight to f6, hitting e4.
White castles — Morphy's move, the main line ever since. The main reply isn't a bishop to c5.
A bishop to c5 is the Møller and a bishop to b5-side is the Archangel; the main move is the modest bishop to e7.
White plays a rook to e1 — and now it actually poses a threat.
At various points in the Ruy, White can capture on c6 and grab e5 — pointless while our e4 is hanging.
But once the rook comes to e1, a capture on c6 followed by a capture on e5 becomes a real threat.
You might think it's time for d6, but first we throw in the very useful b5 — grabbing queenside space and forcing the bishop back.
White retreats to b3. Now e5 is no longer hanging, so d6 isn't forced — the main move d6 just opens the bishop, but we can also play the Marshall Gambit.
We castle, going for the Marshall — not moving the d-pawn, hoping to play d5 in one fell swoop. If White plays c3, we can choose the Marshall with d5 or transpose back to the main line with d6.
White plays c3.
So we play the Marshall Gambit — d5, sacrificing a pawn for a raging initiative.
White captures on d5.
We recapture with the knight on d5.
White grabs on e5 — the gambit is that we've sacrificed it.
We take on e5, and White recaptures with the rook.
Our knight on d5 is hanging, so we have to deal with that threat.
The best move is to defend the knight with a pawn — c6. Defending a piece with a pawn is generally the way forward.
White plays d4. Now we need to chase the rook off e5 — it's in our way — while aiming our pieces at White's king.
So a bishop to d6, chasing the rook knowing that once it moves, our pieces are trained on the white king.
The rook retreats, and we bring the queen into the attack with a queen to h4.

White plays g3, and the queen sinks into h3. This is all theory — I'm rusty on it, and White looks out of book too. Our compensation is clear: a development lead and Swiss-cheese light squares around White's king. If his bishop could reach g2, Black would have nothing — but it can't, so those weak light squares are a lasting problem. The immediate threat is a bishop to g4, hitting the queen.
White plays a knight to d2 — not a main line, sensible but awkward.
Now the bishop can't move, and it does nothing against a bishop to g4 — so let's play it and see where his queen goes.
White plays f3, tremendously weakening — and the moment it's played you should start looking for the typical tactic.
It's not a knight to e3, which just drops the knight — it's a bishop capture on g3. The f3 push weakened g3, a weak link in White's camp.

Sacrificing the bishop on g3 is often low-risk, because we have a perpetual check in our pocket. If you spot a sacrifice that at least guarantees a draw, the risk collapses — you can spend the rest of your time hunting for the win, since a draw beats a loss.

So a bishop capture on g3. If White grabs the light-squared bishop instead he gets mated — a queen to h2, the king to f1, a queen to f2 — so he essentially has to take, and then a queen recapture on g3 gives at least perpetual, though I believe we have more.
White plays a knight to f1 — not testing. A big mistake when sacrificing is forgetting you can simply win material.
A bishop capture on e1 — the rook just hangs! We take it, go up the exchange, and the attack rolls on. Black is winning.
White recaptures on g4.
We could retreat the bishop to h4, but that's plain — a rook to e8 does more, defending the bishop and bringing the rook toward e4 to hit g4, potentially crushing.
White captures on d5.
We recapture on d5. The only reason I put the a-rook on e8 was a possible f5 to open the file — otherwise it doesn't much matter.
White plays a bishop to f4. The f5 idea looks really nice here.
So let's play f5, trying to open the f-file. If White answers g5, we get a passed f-pawn that can later push to f4 and accelerate the attack.
White plays a bishop to e5 — a good move. In such positions it's less about exact moves than following a consistent strategy with healthy attacking moves.
White intercepts with a bishop to h4, so our bishop is attacked and must move — but that's no issue; if we open the file, the game ends fast.
White captures on f5.

We recapture, and the f-file is ours with a million threats — a rook to f2 hitting the queen and threatening mate on g2. Its only drawback is that White can give up material to survive a little longer, so a rook to f8 doubling might finish faster. But if you see a move that wins the queen and you know how to convert, just do it — don't rule out a win because it takes a few extra moves.
You get into trouble when you dismiss options just because they feel slow.
We throw in a rook check on f8 to reposition the rook onto the open file.
The king goes to g1. Now the plan is to eliminate White's defensive resource.

We want to stop White from blocking a check with a piece on g5, so we push the h-pawn to take that square under control — White is totally paralyzed — and then lift a rook to g5 to force the king out.
White plays a rook to d1. The classic mistake would be to reflexively push the h-pawn — but keep your eyes peeled for faster wins, like a queen to g4 winning the rook.
A simple game. At this level the Marshall is a very good weapon against the main-line Ruy Lopez.
We won't dwell on the opening — this isn't an opening course. At the very top, people don't enter the Marshall much anymore; players like Wesley, Duda and Giri prefer the Anti-Marshall.
At the highest level the Marshall is considered to fully equalize for Black — nobody's found anything serious for White — so you'll often see a4 instead.
a4 gets a different kind of position.
You can't play d5 there — it just drops b5.
And after b4, White often goes for d4...
...which gets its own position, again denying Black the d5 Marshall break.
Even ten years ago almost everyone went into the Marshall, and people still do — it's not gone.
Marshall was actually the second person to play it. His original idea wasn't the knight recapture on d5 — he first played it against Frere in 1917, then against Capablanca.
Against Capablanca, in his very first Marshall in a simul, he played a capture on e4 here — still the second-most-popular move, but modern theory says it's just not good for Black.
White captures on c6, Black takes on f3, and White can even grab another pawn.
Despite Black's initiative, there just isn't enough compensation for two pawns.
So a year later, in 1918, Marshall switched to the knight recapture on d5 — but the theory was primitive then.

Everybody up to the 1940s played a knight to f6 after the rook capture, rerouting the knight via g4 — nowadays that's not good. The move c6 was first played only in 1939 by Conel Hugh O'Donel Alexander, who also helped decrypt German communications in the war — the Imitation Game connection. After c6, d4, a bishop to d6, a rook to e1, a queen to h4, g3, a queen to h3, there are two main tries for White: a bishop to e3 and a rook to e4. A knight to d2 is just bad — in our game it's essentially a fatal mistake because of the bishop to g4. Black overwhelms White in the center and on the kingside; if a knight to f3, then a nasty pin with a queen to h5 and a rook to e8 leaves White in ruins. After f3 and the bishop to g3, if White had captured, the winning move is a knight to f4, threatening mate on g2; if he gives up the rook, a bishop capture on f3 and we're winning on material and attack. The engine says White's only try is a rook to e2 giving up the exchange, but after the bishop capture on c2 and a queen to e2, Black is much better. So the Marshall was absolutely not refuted — Marshall just didn't play accurately because the theory was undeveloped. Black is doing great in the Marshall today.
The Anti-Marshall isn't one thing — it's several moves that discourage d5, like h3.
One of them is h3.
And I believe d5 there is inaccurate...
...because after the capture and the knight recapture on d5, White doesn't have to take on e5.
White plays a4 and is supposed to be better, because the c3 square is left open for his knight — that's the key difference.
So after h3, Black should probably revert to a main line, d6 or a bishop to e7 — but check that yourself; I'm not much of a specialist.
